speaker_role: test-prep/consultancy marketer (channel promotes a paid admissions counseling team)
commercial_incentive: Yes - explicitly promotes applying to work with the creator's admissions counseling team (linked in description) and asks viewers to subscribe
key_insights: Argues generic activities (volunteering, joining clubs, playing a sport) fail to differentiate applicants because so many students do the same things, and top schools value uniqueness
Advises seniors close to submitting to rank their three strongest activities and lead with them, since admissions officers reportedly spend only about 7 minutes reviewing an entire application
Introduces a 'vertical vs. horizontal' framework: students should go deep into one interest area (specialize) rather than stacking many shallow, generic activities

Recommends finding a 'unique angle' within a common activity category, e.g. starting your own community-service initiative instead of just volunteering, or building an app instead of just attending a coding club
Stresses proving impact with concrete metrics (downloads, funds raised, members recruited, people helped) rather than vague claims of involvement
Cautions that projects pursued purely for college applications (without genuine interest) tend not to be sustained or convincing
specific_numbers_or_facts: Claims admissions officers spend an average of about 7 minutes reviewing an entire application (unsourced)
notable_or_distinctive: The 'vertical vs horizontal' (skyscraper vs. hundred sheds) metaphor for specializing extracurriculars is a memorable framing, though the underlying advice (depth over breadth, show impact) is common in admissions content.
reliability_notes: The 7-minutes-per-application statistic and other claims are stated without any source; the video ends with a direct pitch for the creator's paid counseling service, indicating a commercial incentive to make admissions sound solvable via their program.
